Introduction

Not all light bulbs are the same. Some get hot, some last for years, and some use much less electricity. In this worksheet you will look at four common types of bulbs and learn the basic differences between them.
Theory

Every light bulb does the same job: it turns electricity into light. But not all bulbs do that equally well. Some bulbs waste a lot of electricity by also turning it into heat. That is why an old-fashioned bulb feels hot after only a minute, while an LED stays cool.
There are four bulb types you will see most often at home and at school. They all use the same electrical socket but they work in completely different ways inside.

INCANDESCENT bulbs (the oldest type) have a thin metal wire inside. When electricity flows through the wire it gets so hot that it glows white. Most of the energy actually becomes heat, not light. These bulbs are no longer sold in most EU countries.
HALOGEN bulbs are an improved version of the incandescent bulb. They contain a small amount of halogen gas which makes the wire last a bit longer and burn slightly brighter. Still mostly heat though.

COMPACT FLUORESCENT (CFL) bulbs use a folded glass tube filled with gas. Electricity makes the gas glow. They use much less electricity than incandescent bulbs but contain a tiny amount of mercury, so they need to be recycled carefully.

LED bulbs (Light Emitting Diode) use a small electronic component that produces light directly when electricity flows through it. They are the most efficient: they convert almost all the electricity into light, and very little into heat. They also last 25 times longer than an incandescent bulb.
Worked example
*How do you read the bulb information table?*
**Step 1:** Look at the row 'Lifetime'. The number tells you how many HOURS the bulb works before it needs to be replaced.
**Step 2:** Example: an LED bulb has a lifetime of 25,000 hours. If you use it 5 hours per day, that is 25,000 ÷ 5 = 5,000 days, which is about 13 years.
**Step 3:** Look at the row 'Wattage'. This tells you how much ELECTRICITY the bulb uses each second it is on. A higher wattage means more electricity.
**Step 4:** Example: an incandescent bulb of 60 W uses 5 times more electricity than an LED of 12 W to give the same amount of light.

Light bulbs differ in three important ways: how much electricity they use, how long they last, and how much they cost to buy. Modern LEDs combine low energy use with a long lifetime, but they are still more expensive to buy than older bulb types. In this worksheet you will quantify these trade-offs.
What you should already know
*You should already know the four common bulb types and what wattage and lifetime mean (see Worksheet 1A if needed).*

All four bulb types in the table give about the same amount of light: 850 lumens. So the only meaningful comparison between them is: how much electricity, money and replacement effort does each one cost to produce that light?
LUMINOUS EFFICACY is the standard way to express how 'good' a light source is at converting electricity into light. It is measured in lumens per watt (lm/W). The formula is:
Efficacy (lm/W) = Light output (lumens) / Power (watts)
Modern LEDs reach 70 to 100 lm/W. An old incandescent bulb only reaches about 14 lm/W. So an LED is roughly 5 to 7 times more efficient.

TOTAL COST OF OWNERSHIP (TCO) is the second key concept. The price you pay in the shop is only part of the cost. You also pay for the electricity the bulb uses and for replacement bulbs when one burns out. To compare two bulb types fairly, you must add all these costs over the same number of hours.
*Calculate the luminous efficacy of a halogen bulb.*
**Step 1:** Read from the table: Halogen produces 850 lumens at 43 W.
**Step 2:** Apply the formula: Efficacy = 850 / 43 ≈ 19.8 lm/W.
**Step 3:** Compare: this is about 1.4 times better than incandescent (850 / 60 ≈ 14.2 lm/W) but about 4 times worse than LED (850 / 12 ≈ 70.8 lm/W).
Luminous efficacy
Lumens of light produced per watt of electricity (lm/W). Higher = better.
Total cost of ownership (TCO)
Purchase cost + electricity cost + replacement cost over the full usage period.
Tariff (τ)
The price of electricity in € per kWh.
kWh
Kilowatt-hour. The unit your electricity company uses for billing. 1 kWh = 1000 W used for 1 hour.

When choosing between light bulbs, the cheapest option depends on how long you use them. For a lamp that is on for only a few minutes per day, an LED may never pay back its higher purchase price. For a lamp that burns 12 hours a day, an LED is far cheaper within a year. In this worksheet you will build a Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) model and analyse when each technology is the rational choice.
*This worksheet assumes you have completed Worksheet 1B (or are confident with luminous efficacy, kWh calculations, and the simple TCO concept).*
At this level we treat bulb selection as an optimisation problem. The TCO function from worksheet 1B can be written more rigorously and analysed mathematically.
The continuous form of TCO over a usage period of t hours is:
TCO(t) ≈ (t / L) · P_bulb + (W · t / 1000) · τ

where L is bulb lifetime (h), P_bulb is the unit purchase price (€), W is the wattage and τ is the electricity tariff (€/kWh). Strictly speaking, you cannot buy 0.7 of a bulb, so the realistic version uses the ceiling function ⌈t/L⌉ for the number of bulbs needed.

BREAK-EVEN ANALYSIS: comparing two bulb types A and B, the break-even hours t\* is the value of t where TCO_A(t) = TCO_B(t). Below t\*, the cheaper-to-buy option wins; above t\*, the more efficient option wins. Solving for t\* algebraically gives insight into when switching technology actually pays off.

SENSITIVITY: real-world conclusions depend on input assumptions (especially τ, which has varied between €0.10 and €0.70 per kWh in the Netherlands in recent years). A robust analysis tests how the conclusion changes when key inputs change.

LIFECYCLE CO₂: the total environmental impact includes both manufacturing emissions (embodied carbon) and emissions from electricity used during the bulb's lifetime. Using the 2024 Dutch grid factor of 0.27 kg CO₂/kWh, manufacturing typically dominates LED lifecycle emissions whereas electricity use dominates incandescent lifecycle emissions.

Building a TCO model
The total cost of ownership over a period of t hours can be written as:
TCO(t) = ⌈t / L⌉ × P_bulb + (W × t / 1000) × τ
where L is the lifetime of one bulb (h), P_bulb is the purchase price (€), W is the wattage (W), τ is the electricity tariff (€/kWh), and ⌈·⌉ is the ceiling function (round up to whole bulbs).
